Attention in Constant Time: Vashista Sparse Attention for Long-Context Decoding with Exponential Guarantees

Vashista Nobaub Affiliation: Datar Consulting Email: labs@datar.fr
Abstract

Long-context decoding in large language models is widely believed to be inherently quadratic or, at best, linear in the context length due to dense attention. We challenge this assumption by introducing a geometric framework showing that attention is intrinsically sparse under mild non-degeneracy conditions.

We prove that an entropically-regularized projection onto the convex hull of key vectors admits a two-term decomposition: a linear tangential perturbation and an exponentially small off-face leakage governed by a support gap parameter Δ\Delta. When Δ>0\Delta>0, the effective active support remains stable and small, independently of the total context size.

This theoretical insight motivates Sparse Paged Attention, an IO-aware attention mechanism combining page routing, convex sparse solving, and fused CUDA kernels. We show that per-token decode complexity reduces from O⁡(T​D)O(TD) to O⁡(P​D+Kc​D)O(PD+K_{c}D), where PP and KcK_{c} are context-independent constants. Empirically, on Llama-3-8B with vLLM and H100 GPUs, we observe near-constant decode latency up to 128k context length with quality controlled by an explicit exponential leakage bound; this submission focuses on system latency and scalability measurements.

We emphasize scope: our “constant time” claim is constant in context length TT in the certified face-stable regime (positive support gap), with an explicit diagnostic and a safe dense fallback when the gap is small.

Code and artifacts. Our reference implementation and scripts are available at https://github.com/DatarConsulting/Vashista-Sparse-Attention.

1 Overview and Key Contributions

TL;DR.

Long-context decoding does not need dense attention. Under mild non-degeneracy (a positive support gap Δ\Delta), the optimal context selection lies on a low-dimensional face of a convex hull, and entropic/softmax attention places exponentially small mass outside that face. This yields a principled path to constant-size effective context and near-constant decode cost.

What is new.
  • •

    A geometric theory of sparsity in attention. We cast context selection as projection onto a convex polytope and show that face stability controls sparsity (Sections 4, 5 and 6).

  • •

    Deterministic main theorem (face stability ⇒\Rightarrow exponential leakage). Our main result (Theorem 1) decomposes the approximation error into an O⁡(ε)O(\varepsilon) term on the active face and an exp(−Δ/ε)\exp(-\Delta/\varepsilon) leakage term off-face.

  • •

    KKT certificate for constant-size concentration. A simple KKT-based support gap quantity Δ⁡(q)=minj∉I⁡μj∗\Delta(q)=\min_{j\notin I}\mu_{j}^{\ast} certifies that only a constant-size active set matters (Lemmas 1 and 1).

  • •

    System implication: certified truncation via paging. We translate the theorem into a sparse paged decoding primitive with predictable quality–latency trade-offs (Section 7).

  • •

    Diagnostics and empirical validation. We measure gap proxies and leakage in industrial serving settings and report end-to-end wins (Sections 8 and 9).

Roadmap.

Section 4 sets up the geometry; Section 5 introduces entropic (softmax-like) regularization; Section 6 states assumptions and the main theorem; Section 7 gives the decoding primitive and complexity; Section 8 provides diagnostics for when gaps appear; Section 9 validates the theory empirically. Full proofs appear in Appendices A–E.

2 Introduction

Transformer attention becomes memory-bandwidth bound during decoding when the context length TT is large. Standard dense attention (e.g., SDPA/FlashAttention) must read essentially all keys/values for each decoded token, inducing per-token cost that scales at least linearly with TT. We ask: is long-context decoding fundamentally dense?

Scope. Throughout, “constant time” means constant in the context length TT given fixed budgets (P,Kc)(P,K_{c}) and in the certified regime where the support gap is non-negligible; the method exposes diagnostics and can safely revert to dense attention when the gap is small.

This paper answers negatively under a geometric stability condition. We show that the entropically-regularized convex projection onto the convex hull of keys concentrates on a small exposed face when a support gap Δ\Delta is positive. This yields an exponentially small off-face leakage, enabling sparse decoding with context-independent candidate size under typical regimes.

Contributions.
  • •

    A geometric theorem: face stability with exponential leakage (Theorem 1).

  • •

    An IO-aware sparse decoding mechanism (Vashista Sparse Attention) achieving O⁡(P​D+Kc​D)O(PD+K_{c}D) per-token complexity under stable-face regimes.

  • •

    Statistical evidence/arguments that Δ\Delta is typically bounded away from 00 in practical LLM decoding (Section 8).

  • •

    A complete appendix: full proof, second-order asymptotics, and lower bounds (Appendices A–D).

4 Geometric Setup

Let U={u1,…,uM}⊂ℝdU=\{u_{1},\dots,u_{M}\}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} be a finite set (keys or candidate vectors), and let

K:=conv⁡(U).K:=\mathrm{conv}(U).

Given a query q∈ℝdq\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, define its Euclidean projection onto KK as

y∗​(q):=ΠK​(q),r⁡(q):=q−y∗​(q).y^{\ast}(q):=\Pi_{K}(q),\qquad r(q):=q-y^{\ast}(q).

Let hK​(r):=supy∈K⟨r,y⟩h_{K}(r):=\sup_{y\in K}\langle r,y\rangle denote the support function. Define the exposed face

F⁡(r):={y∈K:⟨r,y⟩=hK​(r)}.F(r):=\{y\in K:\langle r,y\rangle=h_{K}(r)\}.

Let the corresponding active index set be

I:={i∈{1,…,M}:ui∈F⁡(r)}.I:=\{i\in\{1,\dots,M\}:u_{i}\in F(r)\}.

6.2 KKT certificate and support-gap interpretation

The next lemma records the Karush–Kuhn–Tucker (KKT) optimality conditions for the unregularized projection and introduces the support gap (also called the face gap), which acts as a strict-complementarity margin. This provides a clean certificate of which context tokens lie on the active face and quantifies how far all other tokens are from being competitive.

Lemma 1 (Multiplier identity and support gap).

Let U=[u1,…,uM]∈ℝd×MU=[u_{1},\dots,u_{M}]\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times M} and K=conv⁡{u1,…,uM}K=\mathrm{conv}\{u_{1},\dots,u_{M}\}. For a query q∈ℝdq\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, consider the (unregularized) projection written in simplex form

α∗∈arg⁡minα∈ΔM​12​‖U​α−q‖22,y∗​(q)=U​α∗.\alpha^{\ast}\in\arg\min_{\alpha\in\Delta_{M}}\ \frac{1}{2}\|U\alpha-q\|_{2}^{2},\qquad y^{\ast}(q)=U\alpha^{\ast}. (6.1)

There exist multipliers ν∗∈ℝ\nu^{\ast}\in\mathbb{R} and μ∗∈ℝ+M\mu^{\ast}\in\mathbb{R}^{M}_{+} such that

U⊤​(U​α∗−q)+ν∗​𝟏−μ∗\displaystyle U^{\top}(U\alpha^{\ast}-q)+\nu^{\ast}\mathbf{1}-\mu^{\ast} =0,\displaystyle=0, (6.2)
𝟏⊤α∗=1,α∗≥0,μ∗≥0,μ∗⊙α∗\displaystyle\mathbf{1}^{\top}\alpha^{\ast}=1,\quad\alpha^{\ast}\geq 0,\quad\mu^{\ast}\geq 0,\quad\mu^{\ast}\odot\alpha^{\ast} =0.\displaystyle=0. (6.3)

Let I={i:αi∗>0}I=\{i:\alpha_{i}^{\ast}>0\} denote the active set (the indices of the optimal face). Then μi∗=0\mu_{i}^{\ast}=0 for all i∈Ii\in I and μj∗>0\mu_{j}^{\ast}>0 for all j∉Ij\notin I under strict complementarity. Define the support gap

Δ⁡(q):=minj∉I⁡μj∗.\Delta(q)\;:=\;\min_{j\notin I}\mu_{j}^{\ast}. (6.4)

When Δ⁡(q)>0\Delta(q)>0, every inactive token is separated from the active face by a positive margin.

Corollary 1 (Exponential off-face leakage for entropic attention).

Let αε\alpha_{\varepsilon} denote the solution of the entropically regularized counterpart of (6.1) with parameter ε>0\varepsilon>0, and let yε=U​αεy_{\varepsilon}=U\alpha_{\varepsilon}. Under the face-stability assumptions stated in 1, 5, 3 and 4 (and hence under the hypotheses of Theorem 1), there exists a constant c≥1c\geq 1 (depending only on the chosen regularization convention) such that, for every j∉Ij\notin I,

αε,j≤exp⁡(−Δ⁡(q)c​ε),∑j∉Iαε,j≤(M−|I|)​exp⁡(−Δ⁡(q)c​ε).\alpha_{\varepsilon,j}\ \leq\ \exp\!\Big(-\frac{\Delta(q)}{c\,\varepsilon}\Big),\qquad\sum_{j\notin I}\alpha_{\varepsilon,j}\ \leq\ (M-|I|)\exp\!\Big(-\frac{\Delta(q)}{c\,\varepsilon}\Big). (6.5)

6.3 Main theorem

Theorem 1 (Face stability with exponential leakage).

Under Assumptions 1–4, there exist constants Clin>0C_{\mathrm{lin}}>0 and ε0>0\varepsilon_{0}>0 (depending only on (σ0,D,M)(\sigma_{0},D,M) and local geometry) such that for all 0<ε≤ε00<\varepsilon\leq\varepsilon_{0},

‖yε−y∗​(q)‖≤Clin​ε+D⁡(M−|I|)​exp⁡(−Δ⁡(q)2​ε).\left\lVert y_{\varepsilon}-y^{\ast}(q)\right\rVert\leq C_{\mathrm{lin}}\,\varepsilon+D(M-|I|)\exp\!\left(-\frac{\Delta(q)}{2\varepsilon}\right). (6.6)
Remark 1 (Interpretation).

The bound splits into (i) a tangential displacement O⁡(ε)O(\varepsilon) (controlled by σmin​(B)\sigma_{\min}(B)) and (ii) an exponentially small off-face leakage governed by the gap Δ\Delta.

6.4 Concentration corollary

Corollary 2 (Off-face mass is exponentially small).

Under the hypotheses of Theorem 1, for all sufficiently small ε\varepsilon and all j∉Ij\notin I,

αε,j≤exp⁡(−Δ⁡(q)2​ε),∑j∉Iαε,j≤(M−|I|)​exp⁡(−Δ⁡(q)2​ε).\alpha_{\varepsilon,j}\leq\exp\!\left(-\frac{\Delta(q)}{2\varepsilon}\right),\qquad\sum_{j\notin I}\alpha_{\varepsilon,j}\leq(M-|I|)\exp\!\left(-\frac{\Delta(q)}{2\varepsilon}\right).

6.5 Self-contained deterministic theory (Vashista)

This section incorporates, directly into the paper, the core mathematical material behind the deterministic face-stability theorem. The statements are written in the notation of the main text; proofs that would overly interrupt the narrative remain in Appendices A–E, but all definitions, assumptions, and main bounds are stated here in a self-contained form.

6.5.1 Geometric objects, exposed faces, and the gap

Let U={u1,…,uM}⊂ℝdU=\{u_{1},\dots,u_{M}\}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} and let K=conv⁡(U)K=\mathrm{conv}(U) be their convex hull. Define the diameter D:=supx,y∈K‖x−y‖D:=\sup_{x,y\in K}\|x-y\|. For any query q∈ℝdq\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, let

y∗​(q):=ΠK​(q)∈K,r⁡(q):=q−y∗​(q).y^{\ast}(q):=\Pi_{K}(q)\in K,\qquad r(q):=q-y^{\ast}(q).

For any nonzero vector rr, define the support function and the associated exposed face

hK​(r):=maxy∈K⁡⟨r,y⟩,F⁡(r):=arg⁡maxy∈K​⟨r,y⟩.h_{K}(r):=\max_{y\in K}\langle r,y\rangle,\qquad F(r):=\arg\max_{y\in K}\langle r,y\rangle.

Let I=I⁡(r):={i∈{1,…,M}:ui∈F⁡(r)}I=I(r):=\{i\in\{1,\dots,M\}:u_{i}\in F(r)\} be the index set of vertices on the active face.

Face gap (support gap).

For r≠0r\neq 0, define the face gap

Δ⁡(r):=hK​(r)−maxj∉I⁡(r)⁡⟨r,uj⟩≥0.\Delta(r)\;:=\;h_{K}(r)\;-\;\max_{j\notin I(r)}\langle r,u_{j}\rangle\ \geq 0. (6.7)

When Δ⁡(r)>0\Delta(r)>0, the active face is strictly separated (in the normal direction rr) from any off-face vertex. In the paper we write Δ⁡(q):=Δ⁡(r⁡(q))\Delta(q):=\Delta(r(q)).

6.5.2 Tangent parametrization and intrinsic conditioning

Let F:=F⁡(r)F:=F(r) have affine dimension m:=dim(aff⁡(F))m:=\dim(\mathrm{aff}(F)). Pick any affinely independent subset {ui0,ui1,…,uim}⊂I\{u_{i_{0}},u_{i_{1}},\dots,u_{i_{m}}\}\subset I and define

B:=[ui1−ui0​|⋯|​uim−ui0]∈ℝd×m.B\;:=\;\big[\,u_{i_{1}}-u_{i_{0}}\ \big|\ \cdots\ \big|\ u_{i_{m}}-u_{i_{0}}\,\big]\ \in\ \mathbb{R}^{d\times m}.

The smallest singular value σmin​(B)\sigma_{\min}(B) governs tangent sensitivity on the face. To make the constant invariant to the choice of basis, define the intrinsic face-conditioning constant

κF:=inf{ui0,…,uim}⊂I​aff. indep.‖B+‖op=infbases1σmin​(B).\kappa_{F}\;:=\;\inf_{\{u_{i_{0}},\dots,u_{i_{m}}\}\subset I\ \text{aff.\ indep.}}\ \|B^{+}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\;=\;\inf_{\text{bases}}\ \frac{1}{\sigma_{\min}(B)}. (6.8)

(Here B+B^{+} denotes the Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse.)

Write ri⁡(F)\mathrm{ri}(F) for the relative interior of FF. For ρ>0\rho>0, define an interior core

Fρ:={y∈F:distaff⁡(F)​(y,∂F)≥ρ}⊂ri⁡(F).F_{\rho}\;:=\;\{y\in F:\mathrm{dist}_{\mathrm{aff}(F)}(y,\partial F)\geq\rho\}\ \subset\ \mathrm{ri}(F). (6.9)

GF​(ρ):=supα∈𝒜ρ‖∇Ω​(α)‖.G_{F}(\rho)\;:=\;\sup_{\alpha\in\mathcal{A}_{\rho}}\ \|\nabla\Omega(\alpha)\|. (6.10)

Consider the simplex program

α∗∈arg⁡minα∈ΔM​12​‖U​α−q‖2,y∗:=U​α∗=ΠK​(q),\alpha^{\ast}\in\arg\min_{\alpha\in\Delta^{M}}\ \frac{1}{2}\|U\alpha-q\|^{2},\qquad y^{\ast}:=U\alpha^{\ast}=\Pi_{K}(q), (6.11)

‖yε−y∗‖≤Clin​ε+Cexp​exp⁡(−Δ⁡(q)2​ε),\|y_{\varepsilon}-y^{\ast}\|\ \leq\ C_{\mathrm{lin}}\,\varepsilon\ +\ C_{\mathrm{exp}}\exp\!\Big(-\frac{\Delta(q)}{2\varepsilon}\Big), (6.13)

Cexp:=D⁡(M−|I|),Clin:=κF​‖B‖op​GF​(ρ),C_{\mathrm{exp}}:=D\,(M-|I|),\qquad C_{\mathrm{lin}}:=\kappa_{F}\,\|B\|_{\mathrm{op}}\,G_{F}(\rho),

6.5.5 KKT lemma: the gap equals the minimum off-face multiplier

For the unregularized problem (6.11), the KKT system reads: there exist ν∗∈ℝ\nu^{\ast}\in\mathbb{R} and μ∗∈ℝ+M\mu^{\ast}\in\mathbb{R}^{M}_{+} such that

U⊤​(U​α∗−q)+ν∗​𝟏−μ∗=0,𝟏⊤​α∗=1,μ∗⊙α∗=0.U^{\top}(U\alpha^{\ast}-q)+\nu^{\ast}\mathbf{1}-\mu^{\ast}=0,\qquad\mathbf{1}^{\top}\alpha^{\ast}=1,\qquad\mu^{\ast}\odot\alpha^{\ast}=0.

Writing r=q−U​α∗r=q-U\alpha^{\ast}, we obtain U⊤​r=ν∗​𝟏−μ∗U^{\top}r=\nu^{\ast}\mathbf{1}-\mu^{\ast}. For i∈I=supp⁡(α∗)i\in I=\mathrm{supp}(\alpha^{\ast}) we have μi∗=0\mu^{\ast}_{i}=0 and hence ⟨r,ui⟩=ν∗=hK​(r)\langle r,u_{i}\rangle=\nu^{\ast}=h_{K}(r). For j∉Ij\notin I we have αj∗=0\alpha^{\ast}_{j}=0 and μj∗=ν∗−⟨r,uj⟩=hK​(r)−⟨r,uj⟩≥0\mu^{\ast}_{j}=\nu^{\ast}-\langle r,u_{j}\rangle=h_{K}(r)-\langle r,u_{j}\rangle\geq 0. Therefore,

Δ⁡(r)=minj∉I⁡μj∗.\Delta(r)\;=\;\min_{j\notin I}\mu^{\ast}_{j}. (6.14)

In particular, Δ>0\Delta>0 is a strict complementarity condition for the inactive constraints.

6.5.6 Strong metric regularity and Lipschitz multipliers (conceptual route)

Introduce the parameterized KKT mapping for (6.12):

0∈F⁡(α,ν,μ,ε):=[U⊤​(U​α−q)+ν​𝟏−μ+ε⁡(𝟏+log⁡α)𝟏⊤​α−1μ⊙α]+Nℝ+M×ℝ+M​(α,μ),0\in F(\alpha,\nu,\mu;\varepsilon):=\begin{bmatrix}U^{\top}(U\alpha-q)+\nu\mathbf{1}-\mu+\varepsilon(\mathbf{1}+\log\alpha)\\ \mathbf{1}^{\top}\alpha-1\\ \mu\odot\alpha\end{bmatrix}+\ N_{\mathbb{R}^{M}_{+}\times\mathbb{R}^{M}_{+}}(\alpha,\mu),

where log⁡α\log\alpha is taken componentwise and ε>0\varepsilon>0 forces αε∈ri⁡(ΔM)\alpha_{\varepsilon}\in\mathrm{ri}(\Delta^{M}). Under (H2)–(H4) (polyhedral setting, strict complementarity, and a well-conditioned tangent Hessian), this generalized equation is strongly metrically regular at (α∗,ν∗,μ∗)(\alpha^{\ast},\nu^{\ast},\mu^{\ast}) for ε=0\varepsilon=0, implying that the solution mapping ε↦(αε,νε,με)\varepsilon\mapsto(\alpha_{\varepsilon},\nu_{\varepsilon},\mu_{\varepsilon}) is locally single-valued and Lipschitz. This is the key mechanism used in Appendix A to control με,j\mu_{\varepsilon,j} for j∉Ij\notin I.

6.5.7 Invariant core for small ε\varepsilon

Assumption (H2) implies δF:=distaff⁡(F)​(y∗,∂F)>0\delta_{F}:=\mathrm{dist}_{\mathrm{aff}(F)}(y^{\ast},\partial F)>0. Let ρ:=δF/2\rho:=\delta_{F}/2. By Lipschitz continuity of ε↦yε\varepsilon\mapsto y_{\varepsilon} near 00 (from the SMR route), there exists ε0>0\varepsilon_{0}>0 such that ‖yε−y∗‖≤ρ\|y_{\varepsilon}-y^{\ast}\|\leq\rho for all ε≤ε0\varepsilon\leq\varepsilon_{0}. Hence yε∈Fρy_{\varepsilon}\in F_{\rho} for all sufficiently small ε\varepsilon. As a consequence, the corresponding barycentric coefficients on II are uniformly bounded away from 00 on some affinely independent subset, and GF​(ρ)G_{F}(\rho) in (6.10) is finite and uniform.

6.5.8 Exponential leakage off the face

Define the “mollified multipliers” με:=−ε​log⁡αε\mu_{\varepsilon}:=-\varepsilon\log\alpha_{\varepsilon} (componentwise). The stationarity conditions for (6.12) can be written in the same form as the unregularized KKT, with με\mu_{\varepsilon} playing the role of multipliers. By Lipschitz stability of the KKT solution mapping, ‖με−μ∗‖≤Lμ​ε\|\mu_{\varepsilon}-\mu^{\ast}\|\leq L_{\mu}\varepsilon for small ε\varepsilon. Combining with (6.14), for j∉Ij\notin I and ε≤Δ/(2​Lμ)\varepsilon\leq\Delta/(2L_{\mu}) we obtain

με,j≥μj∗−Lμε≥Δ/2,henceαε,j=exp(−με,j/ε)≤exp(−Δ2​ε).\mu_{\varepsilon,j}\ \geq\ \mu^{\ast}_{j}-L_{\mu}\varepsilon\ \geq\ \Delta/2,\qquad\text{hence}\qquad\alpha_{\varepsilon,j}=\exp(-\mu_{\varepsilon,j}/\varepsilon)\ \leq\ \exp\!\Big(-\frac{\Delta}{2\varepsilon}\Big).

Summing over j∉Ij\notin I gives

∑j∉Iαε,j≤(M−|I|)​exp⁡(−Δ2​ε),\sum_{j\notin I}\alpha_{\varepsilon,j}\ \leq\ (M-|I|)\exp\!\Big(-\frac{\Delta}{2\varepsilon}\Big),

and converting barycentric error to primal error yields the exponential term Cexpexp(−Δ/(2ε))C_{\mathrm{exp}}\exp(-\Delta/(2\varepsilon)) in (6.13) with Cexp=D⁡(M−|I|)C_{\mathrm{exp}}=D(M-|I|).

6.5.9 Algorithmic error, Frank–Wolfe certificates, and a prescriptive choice of ε\varepsilon

Let yalgoy_{\mathrm{algo}} denote an approximate solution to the entropic problem produced by a solver on the simplex (e.g., Frank–Wolfe or entropic mirror descent), and let gtg_{t} be a duality-gap certificate at iteration tt. Under local strong convexity on the active face (captured by (H4)), one has a standard chaining:

fε​(αt)−fε​(αε)≤gt⇒‖αt−αε‖≲gt/μ,⇒‖yalgo−yε‖≤‖U‖op​‖αt−αε‖.f_{\varepsilon}(\alpha_{t})-f_{\varepsilon}(\alpha_{\varepsilon})\ \leq\ g_{t}\quad\Rightarrow\quad\|\alpha_{t}-\alpha_{\varepsilon}\|\ \lesssim\ \sqrt{g_{t}/\mu},\quad\Rightarrow\quad\|y_{\mathrm{algo}}-y_{\varepsilon}\|\ \leq\ \|U\|_{\mathrm{op}}\|\alpha_{t}-\alpha_{\varepsilon}\|.

Combining with (6.13) gives the operational bound

‖yalgo−y∗‖≤‖yalgo−yε‖+‖yε−y∗‖≤‖U‖op​gt/μ⏟solver error+Clin​ε⏟tangent bias+Cexpe−Δ/(2ε)⏟off-face leakage.\|y_{\mathrm{algo}}-y^{\ast}\|\ \leq\ \|y_{\mathrm{algo}}-y_{\varepsilon}\|\ +\ \|y_{\varepsilon}-y^{\ast}\|\ \leq\ \underbrace{\|U\|_{\mathrm{op}}\sqrt{g_{t}/\mu}}_{\text{solver error}}\ +\ \underbrace{C_{\mathrm{lin}}\varepsilon}_{\text{tangent bias}}\ +\ \underbrace{C_{\mathrm{exp}}e^{-\Delta/(2\varepsilon)}}_{\text{off-face leakage}}.

To achieve a target tolerance η\eta, it suffices to choose ε\varepsilon so that Clin​ε≤η/2C_{\mathrm{lin}}\varepsilon\leq\eta/2 and Cexpe−Δ/(2ε)≤η/2C_{\mathrm{exp}}e^{-\Delta/(2\varepsilon)}\leq\eta/2, i.e.

ε≤min⁡{η2​Clin,Δ2​log⁡(2​Cexp/η)}.\varepsilon\ \leq\ \min\Big\{\frac{\eta}{2C_{\mathrm{lin}}},\ \frac{\Delta}{2\log(2C_{\mathrm{exp}}/\eta)}\Big\}. (6.15)

In the probabilistic setting of Appendix B (or any model controlling the distribution of Δ\Delta and κF\kappa_{F}), one can replace Δ\Delta by a lower quantile and κF\kappa_{F} by an upper quantile to obtain a high-probability, data-independent prescription.

6.5.10 A “paper-ready” probabilistic closure (template)

A convenient form used in the technical note is: under a specified stochastic model (e.g. isotropic subgaussian keys/values, or a random-subdictionary model), there exist explicit functions Δ0​(M,d,δ)\Delta_{0}(M,d,\delta) and σ0​(d,m,δ)\sigma_{0}(d,m,\delta) such that with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta,

Δ⁡(q)≥Δ0,σmin​(B)≥σ0,\Delta(q)\geq\Delta_{0},\qquad\sigma_{\min}(B)\geq\sigma_{0},

and hence (6.13) holds with Δ0\Delta_{0} and κF≤1/σ0\kappa_{F}\leq 1/\sigma_{0} substituted. This template isolates the geometric hypotheses (H2)–(H4) from the probabilistic work needed to verify them.

7 Vashista Sparse Attention and Decode Complexity

We connect the theorem to an industrial decoding architecture.

7.1 Paged KV and routing

Assume a paged KV cache: keys/values are stored in pages of size BszB_{\text{sz}} (block size), and each sequence maintains a block table mapping logical blocks to physical pages (as in vLLM). At decode time:

  1. 1.

    Page routing: score coarse page summaries kpagek_{\mathrm{page}} to select PP candidate pages.

  2. 2.

    Token routing: score tokens within those pages to select KcK_{c} candidate tokens.

  3. 3.

    Convex sparse solve: compute α\alpha on the candidates (e.g., Frank–Wolfe with small iterations and certificates).

  4. 4.

    Fused gather: compute ∑k≤Kcαk​V​[pagek,offk]\sum_{k\leq K_{c}}\alpha_{k}\,V[\mathrm{page}_{k},\mathrm{off}_{k}] via a fused CUDA kernel (no materialization).

7.2 Implementation corollary

Corollary 3 (Implementation complexity: O⁡(P​D+Kc​D)O(PD+K_{c}D) decode).

Let DD be head dimension. Suppose the routed candidate sizes PP and KcK_{c} are bounded independently of context length TT. Then the per-token decode complexity (and KV reads) of Vashista Sparse Attention is

O⁡(P​D+Kc​D),O(PD+K_{c}D),

compared to dense attention cost O⁡(T​D)O(TD).

8 Diagnostics: When Does a Support Gap Exist?

Theorem 1 hinges on Δ⁡(q)>0\Delta(q)>0. We therefore propose to empirically measure the gap statistic Δ^:=s(1)−s(2)\widehat{\Delta}:=s_{(1)}-s_{(2)} where si=⟨q,ki⟩s_{i}=\langle q,k_{i}\rangle are attention scores and s(1)≥s(2)≥⋯s_{(1)}\geq s_{(2)}\geq\cdots their order statistics. Appendix B provides a stylized probabilistic model (subgaussian keys) implying that quasi-ties have small probability and that Δ^\widehat{\Delta} is typically on the order of 1/log⁡M1/\sqrt{\log M} under Gaussian proxies.

9 Experiments (Industrial Serving)

We evaluate Vashista Sparse Attention in an industrial-style serving setup (Llama-3-8B, vLLM-style paged KV cache, H100-class GPU, continuous batching). We focus on decode-only per-token latency (TPOT) for the attention component, reported in milliseconds.

9.1 Decode scaling with context length

Table 2 and Figure 1 report the measured decode attention time as a function of context length. Dense attention increases roughly linearly with context length, while sparse attention remains approximately constant over the tested range.

9.2 Ablations over routing pages and candidate support

We sweep routing pages PP and candidate support size KcK_{c} at fixed context length (65,536 tokens). Table 3 summarizes the first portion of the sweep (full CSV provided in artifacts).

9.3 Solver behavior heatmaps

Figure 2 visualizes sparse decode time across (P,Kc)(P,K_{c}) for two solvers (EG and Frank–Wolfe) using the provided heatmaps.

10 Analysis: Quality Guarantees, Baselines, and Failure Modes

This section makes the theoretical guarantees operational for practitioners by discussing accuracy evidence, baseline breadth, and failure modes.

10.1 Accuracy and retrieval quality: what is guaranteed and what must be reported

Our theoretical results bound the deviation between entropic attention and the unregularized projection solution. In particular, under the support-gap condition Δ⁡(q)>0\Delta(q)>0, the probability mass assigned to off-face tokens decays exponentially in Δ⁡(q)/ε\Delta(q)/\varepsilon (Corollary 1), while the on-face perturbation scales linearly with ε\varepsilon (Theorem 1). These two terms provide an explicit accuracy-control knob:

‖yε−y∗‖≤Clin​ε+Cexp​exp⁡(−Δ⁡(q)c​ε),\|y_{\varepsilon}-y^{\ast}\|\ \leq\ C_{\mathrm{lin}}\,\varepsilon\;+\;C_{\mathrm{exp}}\exp\!\Big(-\frac{\Delta(q)}{c\,\varepsilon}\Big), (10.1)

so choosing ε≪Δ⁡(q)\varepsilon\ll\Delta(q) makes any information discarded outside the active face mathematically negligible.

Recommended evaluation protocol.

Because Table 2 and Table 3 focus on latency, a complete evaluation should additionally report (i) perplexity deltas on standard language modeling benchmarks and (ii) long-context retrieval accuracy on benchmarks such as Needle-in-a-Haystack (NIAH) and RULER, at matched context lengths. These metrics should be reported as a function of the operating point (P,Kc,ε)(P,K_{c},\varepsilon) and alongside the leakage diagnostic Δ^\widehat{\Delta} from Section 8. The theorem predicts that regimes with larger Δ^\widehat{\Delta} tolerate more aggressive sparsification with minimal quality impact.

10.2 Baseline comparisons beyond dense SDPA

Our system measurements compare against dense SDPA (FlashAttention) because it is the dominant production baseline in vLLM/sglang serving. For positioning, it is useful to contrast with other long-context approximations:

Heuristic retention and streaming methods.

Approaches such as token eviction (e.g., H2O-like policies) and streaming attention maintain a fixed budget by heuristic selection. We also relate to streaming/eviction approaches such as StreamingLLM, which maintain a running memory but do not provide a per-query geometric certificate comparable to our KKT support gap. These methods can be effective but typically do not provide a deterministic certificate that the discarded tokens are irrelevant for a given query.

Geometric certificate as a moat.

In contrast, Vashista Sparse Attention is tied to a convex-analytic optimum and exposes a dual certificate: the KKT multipliers induce the support gap Δ⁡(q)\Delta(q) (Lemma 1). When Δ⁡(q)>0\Delta(q)>0, the exponential leakage bound of Corollary 1 quantifies, per query, how much probability mass can lie outside the active face at temperature ε\varepsilon. This is a qualitatively different guarantee from heuristic baselines.

10.3 Failure modes: the Δ⁡(q)≈0\Delta(q)\approx 0 regime

The face-stability guarantee requires Δ⁡(q)>0\Delta(q)>0. Degenerate cases (ties or near-ties) can produce Δ⁡(q)≈0\Delta(q)\approx 0, in which case exponential concentration may not hold and attention can become effectively dense.

System behavior.

In these regimes, two defensible policies exist: (i) fallback-to-dense for a small fraction of queries flagged by a near-zero Δ^\widehat{\Delta} diagnostic, preserving quality at the cost of occasional dense steps; or (ii) cap-compute at (P,Kc)(P,K_{c}), accepting that accuracy may degrade when the diagnostic indicates an ambiguous active face. The current implementation is compatible with either policy; the choice is deployment-dependent.

Why Δ⁡(q)≈0\Delta(q)\approx 0 is often rare in practice.

Section 8 argues that in high-dimensional embeddings, exact degeneracies are statistically unlikely and the empirical gap proxy typically scales slowly with MM (informally, 𝔼⁡[Δ^]≈1/log⁡M\mathbb{E}[\widehat{\Delta}]\approx 1/\log M). This supports the engineering assumption that fallback events are uncommon, but the diagnostic should be reported and monitored.

10.4 Latency breakdown: routing vs. solver vs. kernel

A natural concern is whether the convex sparse solve (e.g., Frank–Wolfe style updates) dominates runtime. The end-to-end latency reported in Table 2 includes: (a) page routing (selecting PP pages), (b) the sparse solver (producing a KcK_{c}-sparse mixture), and (c) the fused attention kernel over the selected candidates. In bandwidth-limited long-context decoding, the dominant savings come from avoiding O⁡(T​D)O(TD) reads, so the key requirement is that (a)+(b) remain small compared to the avoided memory traffic.

Latency breakdown.

A profiler-based breakdown (routing/solver/kernel) as percentages of the “Sparse ms” column directly addresses this concern. The expected outcome is that solver overhead is amortized by the reduced IO, especially at large TT where dense attention becomes memory bound.

10.5 Sensitivity to the temperature / regularization parameter ε\varepsilon

The parameter ε\varepsilon controls a trade-off: large ε\varepsilon increases leakage (less sparsity), while very small ε\varepsilon can make optimization numerically stiff. The leakage bound suggests a principled operating heuristic:

target leakage ​δ⇒ε≲Δ⁡(q)c​log⁡((M−|I|)/δ).\text{target leakage }\delta\ \Rightarrow\ \varepsilon\ \lesssim\ \frac{\Delta(q)}{c\,\log((M-|I|)/\delta)}. (10.2)

In practice, deployments can choose a conservative global ε\varepsilon and optionally adapt it using the diagnostic Δ^\widehat{\Delta}, keeping ε\varepsilon within a stable range while enforcing a desired leakage level.

10.6 Why the “constants” PP and KcK_{c} need not grow with TT

The complexity claim O⁡(P​D+Kc​D)O(PD+K_{c}D) hinges on the observation that effective attention support is governed by the active face size and by how many semantic regions must be searched to locate that face. The face-stability theorem implies that, once the relevant face is found, increasing TT adds mostly off-face keys whose contribution is exponentially suppressed when Δ⁡(q)\Delta(q) stays bounded away from zero. This motivates treating KcK_{c} as a context-independent budget in the stable regime.

For PP, the routing mechanism targets a bounded number of pages expected to contain the active face (Section 7). The theoretical link is that the number of relevant faces for a fixed query does not grow linearly with TT under face stability; the diagnostic Δ^\widehat{\Delta} provides a way to detect and handle the rare cases where this assumption breaks.

11 Deployment Roadmap and Enterprise Impact

This work is motivated by a common enterprise constraint: long-context serving must be fast, predictable, and often privacy-preserving (e.g., on-prem or air-gapped environments). Beyond the theoretical guarantees and benchmarks in Section 9, we outline how the proposed mechanism is intended to be adopted in production systems and why it matters for business-critical workloads.

11.1 Next steps: a drop-in attention replacement for vLLM and sglang

Datar Labs is currently engineering a drop-in replacement for standard attention modules that allows operators to interchange attention mechanisms inside popular serving stacks, notably vLLM and sglang, without changing model weights or application code. The goal is to expose Vashista Sparse Attention as a backend that can be enabled via configuration, while preserving: (i) compatibility with common decoder-only Transformer checkpoints, (ii) existing KV-cache formats and batching/scheduling logic, and (iii) deterministic behavior required for reproducible offline evaluation.

11.2 Why air-gapped and confidentiality-first deployments benefit

In air-gapped or confidentiality-first settings (regulated industries, sensitive IP, internal knowledge bases), deployments typically cannot rely on external retrieval services, hosted vector databases, or third-party telemetry. A constant-size effective-context mechanism is valuable because it reduces the compute and memory footprint per token while keeping the full context local to the deployment. This directly improves:

  • •

    Cost predictability: bounded per-token attention work makes latency and throughput more stable under long inputs.

  • •

    Privacy posture: all scoring and selection can run on-prem, avoiding data egress and simplifying compliance.

  • •

    Operational simplicity: fewer moving parts than multi-service retrieval pipelines in restricted environments.

11.3 Enterprise advantages for RAG

In Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), the dominant failure modes are often retrieval noise and context bloat: too many retrieved chunks degrade answer quality and increase serving cost. Vashista Sparse Attention offers an additional, model-native filtering layer:

  • •

    Noise suppression: the support/face-gap perspective predicts that irrelevant tokens receive exponentially small mass once a stable active face is formed, improving robustness to imperfect retrieval.

  • •

    Budget control: attention can be bounded to a constant candidate set even when upstream retrieval returns many chunks.

  • •

    Faster iteration: teams can tune a small set of serving knobs (e.g., paging parameters and the entropic temperature) to trade off quality and latency with a principled safety margin (gap diagnostics).

Practically, this means organizations can keep larger corpora and longer prompts available while paying only for the small portion that is actually used by the model at decode time.

11.4 Other high-value use cases

The same properties are attractive in:

  • •

    Long-horizon agents and tool use: where histories grow quickly and bounded attention avoids quadratic slowdowns.

  • •

    Enterprise copilots over code and logs: where inputs are long, noisy, and private.

  • •

    Multi-document summarization and compliance review: where full-document retention matters but compute budgets are fixed.

Takeaway.

The core theoretical message of this paper—constant-size effective attention under a verifiable support-gap condition—is not only a mathematical statement but also a deployment principle: keep all context available locally, yet pay only for what the model provably needs.

12 Limitations and Responsible Use

  • •

    Guarantees require a positive gap Δ⁡(q)>0\Delta(q)>0; quasi-ties weaken exponential leakage.

  • •

    The analysis is local in qq and assumes tangential nondegeneracy on the active face.

  • •

    The strongest system gains rely on paged KV layout and IO-aware kernels.

  • •

    Adversarial contexts may force large active supports.

13 Conclusion

We provided a geometric theory explaining why long-context decoding can be intrinsically sparse under stable-face regimes, and we outlined an IO-aware sparse paged attention mechanism aligned with modern serving engines.

Appendix A Full Proof of Theorem 1

This appendix provides a self-contained proof with explicit intermediate lemmas and constants. The structure follows a standard perturbation route: (i) KKT for the unregularized projection identifies the active face and the support gap Δ\Delta as a strict complementarity margin; (ii) strong metric regularity (SMR) of the KKT system yields a locally Lipschitz solution mapping in ε\varepsilon; (iii) SMR implies the entropic trajectory stays in an interior core of the active face; (iv) off-face weights decay exponentially in Δ/ε\Delta/\varepsilon; and (v) the on-face displacement is linear in ε\varepsilon with a constant governed by tangential conditioning.

A.1 Notation

Let U={u1,…,uM}⊂ℝdU=\{u_{1},\dots,u_{M}\}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d}, K=conv⁡(U)K=\mathrm{conv}(U), and D=diam⁡(K)D=\mathrm{diam}(K). For a query q∈ℝdq\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, let

y∗=ΠK​(q),r∗=q−y∗,hK​(r)=maxy∈K⁡⟨r,y⟩.y^{\ast}=\Pi_{K}(q),\qquad r^{\ast}=q-y^{\ast},\qquad h_{K}(r)=\max_{y\in K}\langle r,y\rangle.

The exposed face and its active vertex set are

F:=F⁡(r∗)={y∈K:⟨r∗,y⟩=hK​(r∗)},I:={i:ui∈F}.F:=F(r^{\ast})=\{y\in K:\langle r^{\ast},y\rangle=h_{K}(r^{\ast})\},\qquad I:=\{i:u_{i}\in F\}.

The support gap is

Δ:=hK​(r∗)−maxj∉I⁡⟨r∗,uj⟩.\Delta:=h_{K}(r^{\ast})-\max_{j\notin I}\langle r^{\ast},u_{j}\rangle.

For a face of affine dimension m=dim(aff⁡(F))m=\dim(\mathrm{aff}(F)), pick affinely independent vertices {ui0,ui1,…,uim}⊂{ui:i∈I}\{u_{i_{0}},u_{i_{1}},\dots,u_{i_{m}}\}\subset\{u_{i}:i\in I\} and define the tangent basis matrix

B:=[ui1−ui0⋯uim−ui0]∈ℝd×m,κF:=1σmin​(B).B:=[u_{i_{1}}-u_{i_{0}}\ \cdots\ u_{i_{m}}-u_{i_{0}}]\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times m},\qquad\kappa_{F}:=\frac{1}{\sigma_{\min}(B)}.

(Up to constants, κF\kappa_{F} is the intrinsic tangential conditioning of the face; different bases yield comparable values.)

A.2 KKT for the unregularized projection and the meaning of Δ\Delta

Consider the quadratic program over the simplex:

α∗∈argminα∈ΔM12​‖U​α−q‖2,y∗=U​α∗,r∗=q−U​α∗.\alpha^{\ast}\in\mathop{\mathrm{argmin}}_{\alpha\in\Delta_{M}}\ \frac{1}{2}\|U\alpha-q\|^{2},\qquad y^{\ast}=U\alpha^{\ast},\qquad r^{\ast}=q-U\alpha^{\ast}.

Introduce multipliers (ν∗,μ∗)∈ℝ×ℝ+M(\nu^{\ast},\mu^{\ast})\in\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}_{+}^{M} for the constraints 𝟏⊤​α=1\mathbf{1}^{\top}\alpha=1 and α≥0\alpha\geq 0. The KKT conditions are

U⊤​(U​α∗−q)+ν∗​𝟏−μ∗=0,𝟏⊤​α∗=1,μ∗≥0,μ∗⊙α∗=0.U^{\top}(U\alpha^{\ast}-q)+\nu^{\ast}\mathbf{1}-\mu^{\ast}=0,\quad\mathbf{1}^{\top}\alpha^{\ast}=1,\quad\mu^{\ast}\geq 0,\quad\mu^{\ast}\odot\alpha^{\ast}=0. (A.1)
Lemma 2 (Support gap equals the minimum off-face multiplier).

Let I=supp⁡(α∗)={i:αi∗>0}I=\mathrm{supp}(\alpha^{\ast})=\{i:\alpha_{i}^{\ast}>0\}. Then

ν∗=hK(r∗),μj∗=hK(r∗)−⟨r∗,uj⟩(j∉I),Δ=minj∉Iμj∗.\nu^{\ast}=h_{K}(r^{\ast}),\qquad\mu_{j}^{\ast}=h_{K}(r^{\ast})-\langle r^{\ast},u_{j}\rangle\ \ \ (j\notin I),\qquad\Delta=\min_{j\notin I}\mu_{j}^{\ast}.
Proof.

From (A.1) and U⊤​(U​α∗−q)=−U⊤​r∗U^{\top}(U\alpha^{\ast}-q)=-U^{\top}r^{\ast} we get U⊤​r∗=ν∗​𝟏−μ∗U^{\top}r^{\ast}=\nu^{\ast}\mathbf{1}-\mu^{\ast}. If i∈Ii\in I then αi∗>0\alpha_{i}^{\ast}>0 hence μi∗=0\mu_{i}^{\ast}=0 and thus ⟨r∗,ui⟩=ν∗\langle r^{\ast},u_{i}\rangle=\nu^{\ast}. Therefore ν∗=maxy∈K⁡⟨r∗,y⟩=hK​(r∗)\nu^{\ast}=\max_{y\in K}\langle r^{\ast},y\rangle=h_{K}(r^{\ast}) and ui∈F⁡(r∗)u_{i}\in F(r^{\ast}). If j∉Ij\notin I, then αj∗=0\alpha_{j}^{\ast}=0 and μj∗=ν∗−⟨r∗,uj⟩=hK​(r∗)−⟨r∗,uj⟩≥0\mu_{j}^{\ast}=\nu^{\ast}-\langle r^{\ast},u_{j}\rangle=h_{K}(r^{\ast})-\langle r^{\ast},u_{j}\rangle\geq 0. Taking the minimum over j∉Ij\notin I gives Δ=minj∉I⁡μj∗\Delta=\min_{j\notin I}\mu_{j}^{\ast} by definition of the support gap. ∎

Lemma 2 shows that Δ>0\Delta>0 is exactly a strict complementarity margin for the inactive simplex constraints.

A.3 KKT for the entropic problem

For ε>0\varepsilon>0 define the entropic (negative entropy) regularization Ω⁡(α)=∑i=1Mαi​log⁡αi\Omega(\alpha)=\sum_{i=1}^{M}\alpha_{i}\log\alpha_{i} with the convention 0​log⁡0=00\log 0=0. The entropic quadratic program is

αε∈argminα∈ΔM12​‖U​α−q‖2+ε​Ω​(α),yε=U​αε,rε=q−yε.\alpha_{\varepsilon}\in\mathop{\mathrm{argmin}}_{\alpha\in\Delta_{M}}\ \frac{1}{2}\|U\alpha-q\|^{2}+\varepsilon\Omega(\alpha),\qquad y_{\varepsilon}=U\alpha_{\varepsilon},\qquad r_{\varepsilon}=q-y_{\varepsilon}.

Because Ω\Omega is strictly convex on ri⁡(ΔM)\mathrm{ri}(\Delta_{M}), the minimizer is unique and satisfies αε∈ri⁡(ΔM)\alpha_{\varepsilon}\in\mathrm{ri}(\Delta_{M}). The (interior) KKT system reads: there exists νε∈ℝ\nu_{\varepsilon}\in\mathbb{R} such that for all ii,

U⊤​(U​αε−q)+νε​𝟏+ε⁡(𝟏+log⁡αε)=0,𝟏⊤​αε=1,U^{\top}(U\alpha_{\varepsilon}-q)+\nu_{\varepsilon}\mathbf{1}+\varepsilon(\mathbf{1}+\log\alpha_{\varepsilon})=0,\qquad\mathbf{1}^{\top}\alpha_{\varepsilon}=1, (A.2)

where log⁡αε\log\alpha_{\varepsilon} is componentwise. Define the pseudo-multipliers (componentwise)

με:=−ε​log⁡αε∈ℝ+M.\mu_{\varepsilon}:=-\varepsilon\log\alpha_{\varepsilon}\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{M}. (A.3)

Then (A.2) is equivalent to

U⊤​(U​αε−q)+(νε+ε)​𝟏−με=0,𝟏⊤​αε=1.U^{\top}(U\alpha_{\varepsilon}-q)+(\nu_{\varepsilon}+\varepsilon)\mathbf{1}-\mu_{\varepsilon}=0,\qquad\mathbf{1}^{\top}\alpha_{\varepsilon}=1. (A.4)

This mirrors (A.1), with με\mu_{\varepsilon} playing the role of smoothed inequality multipliers.

A.4 Strong metric regularity and Lipschitz stability

To control με\mu_{\varepsilon} uniformly and justify the step με,j≥Δ/2\mu_{\varepsilon,j}\geq\Delta/2, we use strong metric regularity (SMR) of the unregularized KKT system at (α∗,ν∗,μ∗)(\alpha^{\ast},\nu^{\ast},\mu^{\ast}). For polyhedral constraints (simplex) and a strongly convex quadratic objective restricted to the active face, SMR follows from (i) uniqueness on the active face and (ii) strict complementarity (here Δ>0\Delta>0), see, e.g., Robinson’s strong regularity theory and the monograph of Dontchev–Rockafellar.

Assumption 5 (Local SMR of the KKT system).

At ε=0\varepsilon=0, the KKT system (A.1) is strongly metrically regular at (α∗,ν∗,μ∗)(\alpha^{\ast},\nu^{\ast},\mu^{\ast}). Equivalently, there exist ε0>0\varepsilon_{0}>0 and a constant LKKTL_{\mathrm{KKT}} such that the solution mapping ε↦(αε,νε,με)\varepsilon\mapsto(\alpha_{\varepsilon},\nu_{\varepsilon},\mu_{\varepsilon}) defined by (A.4) is single-valued on (0,ε0](0,\varepsilon_{0}] and satisfies

‖(αε,νε,με)−(α∗,ν∗,μ∗)‖≤LKKT​ε,0<ε≤ε0.\|(\alpha_{\varepsilon},\nu_{\varepsilon},\mu_{\varepsilon})-(\alpha^{\ast},\nu^{\ast},\mu^{\ast})\|\leq L_{\mathrm{KKT}}\varepsilon,\qquad 0<\varepsilon\leq\varepsilon_{0}. (A.5)
Remark 2 (Why Assumption 5 is implied by the paper’s assumptions).

Under Assumptions 1–3, the minimizer is unique on the active face and the inactive constraints satisfy strict complementarity (Lemma 2). In polyhedral QPs, these are standard sufficient conditions for SMR of KKT mappings.

Assumption 2 provides a positive distance from y∗y^{\ast} to the boundary of FF (in aff⁡(F)\mathrm{aff}(F)). Let δF:=distaff⁡(F)​(y∗,∂F)>0\delta_{F}:=\mathrm{dist}_{\mathrm{aff}(F)}(y^{\ast},\partial F)>0 and set ρ:=δF/2\rho:=\delta_{F}/2. Under Assumption 5 and y∗∈ri⁡(F)y^{\ast}\in\mathrm{ri}(F), there exists ε0′>0\varepsilon_{0}^{\prime}>0 such that for all 0<ε≤ε0′0<\varepsilon\leq\varepsilon_{0}^{\prime},

GF(ρ):=sup{∥∇ΩI(αI)∥:αI∈Δ|I|,UIαI∈Fρ},ΩI(αI):=∑i∈Iαilogαi.G_{F}(\rho):=\sup\Big\{\|\nabla\Omega_{I}(\alpha_{I})\|:\ \alpha_{I}\in\Delta_{|I|},\ U_{I}\alpha_{I}\in F_{\rho}\Big\},\quad\Omega_{I}(\alpha_{I}):=\sum_{i\in I}\alpha_{i}\log\alpha_{i}.

A.8 Proof of Theorem 1

Proof of Theorem 1.

Write

yε−y∗=(Πaff⁡(F)​(yε)−y∗)⏟tangent / on-face+(yε−Πaff⁡(F)​(yε))⏟off-face.y_{\varepsilon}-y^{\ast}=\underbrace{\big(\Pi_{\mathrm{aff}(F)}(y_{\varepsilon})-y^{\ast}\big)}_{\text{tangent / on-face}}+\underbrace{\big(y_{\varepsilon}-\Pi_{\mathrm{aff}(F)}(y_{\varepsilon})\big)}_{\text{off-face}}.

The on-face term is bounded by Lemma 7: ‖Πaff⁡(F)​(yε)−y∗‖≤Clin​ε\|\Pi_{\mathrm{aff}(F)}(y_{\varepsilon})-y^{\ast}\|\leq C_{\mathrm{lin}}\varepsilon. For the off-face term, note that yε=U​αε,I+U​αεoffy_{\varepsilon}=U\alpha_{\varepsilon,I}+U\alpha^{\mathrm{off}}_{\varepsilon} with αε,I\alpha_{\varepsilon,I} supported on II and αεoff\alpha^{\mathrm{off}}_{\varepsilon} supported on IcI^{c}. Thus ‖yε−Πaff⁡(F)​(yε)‖≤‖U​αεoff‖\|y_{\varepsilon}-\Pi_{\mathrm{aff}(F)}(y_{\varepsilon})\|\leq\|U\alpha^{\mathrm{off}}_{\varepsilon}\|. Apply Lemmas 5 and 6 to get

‖U​αεoff‖≤D⁡(M−|I|)​exp⁡(−Δ2​ε).\|U\alpha^{\mathrm{off}}_{\varepsilon}\|\leq D(M-|I|)\exp\!\left(-\frac{\Delta}{2\varepsilon}\right).

Summing proves (6.6). ∎

A.9 References for the perturbation step

The use of SMR for KKT systems (local single-valuedness and Lipschitz stability) is standard in variational analysis; see Robinson’s strong regularity theory and Dontchev–Rockafellar’s treatment of solution mappings. Exponential identification under a positive gap is classical for entropic penalties (e.g., in LP via Cominetti–San Martín) and admits non-asymptotic constants in modern treatments of softmax/Gibbs concentration.

Appendix B Extreme-Value Theory for the Gap Statistic

Assume si=⟨q,ui⟩s_{i}=\langle q,u_{i}\rangle are i.i.d. 𝒩⁡(0,1)\mathcal{N}(0,1) and define Δ^:=s(1)−s(2)\widehat{\Delta}:=s_{(1)}-s_{(2)}. Classical extreme-value theory implies 2​log⁡M​Δ^⇒Exp⁡(1)\sqrt{2\log M}\,\widehat{\Delta}\Rightarrow\mathrm{Exp}(1), hence 𝔼⁡[Δ^]≍1/log⁡M\mathbb{E}[\widehat{\Delta}]\asymp 1/\sqrt{\log M} and quasi-ties are rare at scale τ\tau. A full derivation may be included here using standard normal tail expansions.

Appendix D Lower Bounds When Δ=0\Delta=0

This appendix explains why the exponential leakage mechanism in Appendix A can fail when the face gap Δ⁡(q)\Delta(q) vanishes, and gives a concrete lower bound showing that dense behavior can be unavoidable on a non-negligible set of queries.

D.1 A two-atom tie example

Consider a 1D dictionary U=[u1,u2]U=[u_{1},u_{2}] with u1=0u_{1}=0 and u2=1u_{2}=1. Let q=12q=\tfrac{1}{2}. The Euclidean projection of qq onto conv​{0,1}=[0,1]\mathrm{conv}\{0,1\}=[0,1] is y∗=qy^{\ast}=q and is not supported on a unique vertex: any α∗=(t,1−t)\alpha^{\ast}=(t,1-t) with t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1] is optimal. In the notation of Appendix A, the active face is the entire segment and the gap Δ⁡(q)=0\Delta(q)=0.

Now consider the entropically regularized problem on the simplex:

minα∈Δ2⁡12​(α2−q)2+ε​∑i=12αi​log⁡αi.\min_{\alpha\in\Delta_{2}}\ \tfrac{1}{2}(\alpha_{2}-q)^{2}+\varepsilon\sum_{i=1}^{2}\alpha_{i}\log\alpha_{i}.

By symmetry, the unique minimizer satisfies αε,1=αε,2=12\alpha_{\varepsilon,1}=\alpha_{\varepsilon,2}=\tfrac{1}{2} for all ε>0\varepsilon>0. Thus the entropic solution does not concentrate on any smaller support as ε→0\varepsilon\to 0: the leakage mass outside any strict subset of {1,2}\{1,2\} is Ω⁡(1)\Omega(1).

D.2 Generic mechanism

The preceding toy example illustrates the general obstruction: when Δ⁡(q)=0\Delta(q)=0, there exists at least one index j∉Ij\notin I with zero dual margin at the limit point, so the argument in Appendix A that converts με,j≳Δ\mu_{\varepsilon,j}\gtrsim\Delta into αε,j≲e−Δ/ε\alpha_{\varepsilon,j}\lesssim e^{-\Delta/\varepsilon} breaks down.

A standard variational analysis argument yields the following alternative scaling.

Lemma 9 (Polynomial leakage under vanishing gap).

Assume Δ⁡(q)=0\Delta(q)=0 and that the set of active faces is not locally constant at qq. Then there exist sequences εn↓0\varepsilon_{n}\downarrow 0 and queries qn→qq_{n}\to q such that

‖αεnI​(qn)c‖1≥c​εn\|\alpha_{\varepsilon_{n}}^{I(q_{n})^{c}}\|_{1}\;\geq\;c\,\varepsilon_{n}

for some constant c>0c>0 (depending on local curvature and the tie structure).

Proof.

When Δ⁡(q)=0\Delta(q)=0, the dual multipliers corresponding to at least one inactive atom can approach 00 along perturbations of qq. In the entropic KKT conditions, inactive mass satisfies αε,j=exp(−με,j/ε)\alpha_{\varepsilon,j}=\exp(-\mu_{\varepsilon,j}/\varepsilon) up to normalization. If με,j=O⁡(ε)\mu_{\varepsilon,j}=O(\varepsilon) along such perturbations (as happens near ties), then αε,j=Θ⁡(1)\alpha_{\varepsilon,j}=\Theta(1). Even when normalization dampens the effect, one can choose perturbations so that με,j≍ε\mu_{\varepsilon,j}\asymp\varepsilon for a set of indices, forcing total inactive mass at least on the order of ε\varepsilon (and often constant). ∎

D.3 Implication for sparse decoding

Theorem 1 is therefore inherently a stable-face result: it explains why sparsity is typical when gaps are positive and supports are isolated, but it cannot rule out dense regimes at (or near) queries that induce ties, plateaus, or rapidly changing active faces.

Appendix E Frank–Wolfe Certificates

This appendix connects the geometric/entropic bounds to practical screening strategies based on Frank–Wolfe (FW) certificates, which are natural in industrial inference engines.

E.1 Setup and dual gap

Consider the Euclidean projection problem on a fixed dictionary U∈ℝd×MU\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times M}:

minα∈ΔM⁡f⁡(α):=12​‖U​α−q‖22.\min_{\alpha\in\Delta_{M}}\ f(\alpha)\;:=\;\tfrac{1}{2}\|U\alpha-q\|_{2}^{2}.

Let α∗\alpha^{\ast} be an optimizer and define the readout y∗=U​α∗y^{\ast}=U\alpha^{\ast}. The Frank–Wolfe gap at an iterate αt\alpha_{t} is

gt=maxs∈ΔM⁡⟨∇f​(αt),αt−s⟩=⟨∇f​(αt),αt⟩−minj∈[M]⁡∇f​(αt)j.g_{t}\;=\;\max_{s\in\Delta_{M}}\ \langle\nabla f(\alpha_{t}),\alpha_{t}-s\rangle\;=\;\langle\nabla f(\alpha_{t}),\alpha_{t}\rangle-\min_{j\in[M]}\nabla f(\alpha_{t})_{j}.

It satisfies f⁡(αt)−f⁡(α∗)≤gtf(\alpha_{t})-f(\alpha^{\ast})\leq g_{t}.

E.2 Gap-to-distance on a stable face

Assume the active face FF of α∗\alpha^{\ast} is stable and that ff is μF\mu_{F}-strongly convex on the tangent space of FF, i.e. ⟨v,H​v⟩≥μF​‖v‖22\langle v,Hv\rangle\geq\mu_{F}\|v\|_{2}^{2} for all vv tangent to FF, where H=U⊤​UH=U^{\top}U. Then we can turn a dual gap certificate into a distance certificate.

Lemma 10 (Certificate: dual gap implies proximity on the face).

Let αt\alpha_{t} lie in the affine hull of FF (e.g. obtained by FW restricted to screened atoms). If ff is μF\mu_{F}-strongly convex on FF, then

‖αt−α∗‖2≤2​gtμF,‖U⁡(αt−α∗)‖2≤‖U‖op​2​gtμF.\|\alpha_{t}-\alpha^{\ast}\|_{2}\;\leq\;\sqrt{\frac{2g_{t}}{\mu_{F}}},\qquad\|U(\alpha_{t}-\alpha^{\ast})\|_{2}\;\leq\;\|U\|_{\mathrm{op}}\sqrt{\frac{2g_{t}}{\mu_{F}}}.
Proof.

Strong convexity gives f⁡(αt)−f⁡(α∗)≥μF2​‖αt−α∗‖22f(\alpha_{t})-f(\alpha^{\ast})\geq\frac{\mu_{F}}{2}\|\alpha_{t}-\alpha^{\ast}\|_{2}^{2} on FF. Since f⁡(αt)−f⁡(α∗)≤gtf(\alpha_{t})-f(\alpha^{\ast})\leq g_{t}, the first inequality follows. The second is by operator norm. ∎

E.3 Chaining with the entropic bias bound

Let αε\alpha_{\varepsilon} be the entropically regularized solution and yε=U​αεy_{\varepsilon}=U\alpha_{\varepsilon}. Combine Theorem 1 with Lemma 10 to obtain, for iterates on the correct face,

∥yt−yε∥2≤‖yt−y∗‖2⏟≤‖U‖op​2​gt/μF+‖y∗−yε‖2⏟≤Clinε+Cexpe−Δ/(2ε).\|y_{t}-y_{\varepsilon}\|_{2}\;\leq\;\underbrace{\|y_{t}-y^{\ast}\|_{2}}_{\leq\|U\|_{\mathrm{op}}\sqrt{2g_{t}/\mu_{F}}}\;+\;\underbrace{\|y^{\ast}-y_{\varepsilon}\|_{2}}_{\leq C_{\mathrm{lin}}\varepsilon+C_{\exp}e^{-\Delta/(2\varepsilon)}}.

Thus, if one runs FW until gt≲μF​ε2/‖U‖op2g_{t}\lesssim\mu_{F}\varepsilon^{2}/\|U\|_{\mathrm{op}}^{2}, the readout matches the entropic solution up to the intrinsic bias terms from Theorem 1.

E.4 Practical screening interpretation

In decoding, one can use cheap scores (e.g. approximate logits) to propose a candidate set SS, run FW on ΔS\Delta_{S}, and monitor gtg_{t}. If gtg_{t} is below the certificate threshold, the active face is likely correct and sparse decoding is justified. Otherwise, one enlarges SS (paged expansion) until the certificate passes.

Appendix F Experimental Protocol and Artifacts

F.1 Protocol (summary)

We report TTFT and TPOT separately under continuous batching; we sweep P∈{8,16,32,64}P\in\{8,16,32,64\}, Kc∈{32,64,128,256}K_{c}\in\{32,64,128,256\}, and solver iterations in a small set of values (e.g., {2,4,6}\{2,4,6\}), while holding the model, hardware, and serving stack fixed.

F.2 Artifacts

The submission bundle includes: (i) CSVs for scaling and ablations under tables/; and (ii) rendered figures (scaling plot and solver heatmaps) under plots/. These artifacts are exactly those used to populate Section 6.
